faqs.q: What is an annualised wage and how does it affect my salary increase?
faqs.a: An annualised wage is a fixed regular amount paid each year that covers minimum pay, penalties, overtime, allowances, and annual leave loading. Awards often require a review every 12 months to ensure the employee received at least the award entitlements. If the annualised wage falls short, the employer must pay the difference. This review process can influence how much your salary should increase each year in Australia, as it ensures compliance with award rates.

faqs.q: How is casual loading calculated and does it affect my annual salary?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% on top of the base hourly rate, as per the National Minimum Wage and many awards. For example, the minimum casual rate from 1 July 2026 is $33.05 per hour. When converting to annual salary, you multiply the casual rate by 38 hours per week and 52 weeks. The loading compensates for lack of paid leave entitlements like annual leave and personal leave.

faqs.q: How does superannuation impact my take-home pay and salary increase expectations?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% of ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. It is not part of your salary but an additional contribution. When asking 'how much should my salary increase each year Australia, remember that super is separate. Your salary increase discussions are typically on base pay, not super is on top.

bodyMarkdown:
## How to Convert Hourly Rate to Annual Salary

When you know your hourly rate, converting to an annual salary is straightforward. The standard formula is hourly rate multiplied by hours per week multiplied by 52 weeks. For full-time employees, we assume a 38-hour week, which is the standard under the National Employment Standards. This gives you a gross annual figure before tax and super.

### The Formula

Annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 hours × 52 weeks. For example, if your hourly rate is $30, your annual salary is $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no allowances. If you work part-time, adjust the hours per week accordingly.

### Fortnightly Pay

Many employers pay fortnightly. Your fortnightly gross pay is your weekly pay multiplied by 2. Weekly pay is hourly rate × 38. So fortnightly = hourly rate × 38 × 2. Using the same $30 rate, fortnightly gross is $30 × 38 × 2 = $2,280. This helps when budgeting or comparing job offers.

### Understanding Minimum Wage and Awards and Casual Loading

The National Minimum Wage from 1 July 2026 is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Most employees are covered by an award that sets higher minimum rates. Awards also include penalty rates, overtime, and allowances. If you are a casual employee, you receive a 25% casual loading on top of the base rate. For the minimum wage, that is $33.05 per hour. When using our [the timesheet](/), you can check the box to add 25% casual loading. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading; the tool adds it for you.

### Superannuation Paid on Top

Super guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid by your employer on top of your salary. It is not deducted from your pay. The maximum contribution base is $270,830 per year. For example, on a $60,000 salary, your employer contributes $7,200 super. Your total remuneration is $67,200, but your take-home pay is based on the $60,000. When considering how much your salary should increase each year in Australia, remember that super increases are separate from base salary negotiations.

### Tax and Medicare

Your annual salary is taxed using the 2026–27 resident tax rates: nil up to $18,200, 15% from $18,201 to $45,000, 30% to $135,000, 37% to $190,000, and 45% above that. The Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. This calculator uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds for Medicare because the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed. Tax is estimated based on the full tax-free threshold. No HELP, Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging is deducted. For a detailed estimate, use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool.

### How Much Should My Salary Increase Each Year Australia?

There is no legal requirement for a salary increase each year unless your award or agreement specifies one. However, the Fair Work Commission reviews the National Minimum Wage annually, often resulting in an increase. Awards also have annual wage reviews. The Fair Work Ombudsman notes that annualised wage arrangements must be reviewed every 12 months to ensure the employee received at least the award entitlements. If the arrangement falls short, the employer must pay the difference. This review process can effectively increase your pay if your annualised wage was too low. For most employees, salary increases depend on performance, market rates, or enterprise agreements. Use our [pay guides](/blog) to check award rates and see if you are due for a raise.

### Using the Hourly to Annual Calculator

Our [the timesheet](/) lets you enter your base hourly rate and choose whether to add casual loading. It then calculates your annual salary, fortnightly pay, estimated tax, Medicare, and super. The results are estimates based on standard assumptions. Always check your actual pay slip and consult the Fair Work Ombudsman for your specific award.

### Summary

Converting hourly to annual is simple: hourly × 38 × 52. Add casual loading if applicable. Super is on top. Tax and Medicare reduce your take-home pay. When asking 'how much should my salary increase each year Australia', consider award reviews, annualised wage reviews, and your employment contract.
